porbos.title: Three Doors Before War • The Woman Who Was Not Fighting • The Question in the Dark of Night • The Old Man, the Worshipper and the Fruit-Bearing Tree • Did You Split Open His Heart? • An Open Declaration Is Enough

blocks.1: In pre-Islamic Arabia there was no declaration of war. In the last watch of the night, the sound of horses’ hooves, then shouting. Waking up, one would find a tent on fire, another would see their herd of camels being driven off by men of another tribe. The opponent was not asked anything. What do you want, why have you come, is there any other way; there was no place for such questions. The sword was the first word, the sword was the last.
blocks.2: The Prophet {{1}} set an order even for war. When sending out any army he would tell the commander separately to fear Allah, and to treat his companions well. Then would come the matter of the enemy. Buraydah ibn al-Husayb (RA) remembered that instruction,
blocks.4: When you meet your enemy from among the polytheists, call them to three matters. Whichever of them they respond to, accept it, and hold your hand back from harming them. First call them to Islam; if they respond, accept it, hold back your hand. If they do not agree, ask them for the jizyah; if they agree to pay, accept it, hold back your hand. If they do not agree even to that, seek Allah’s help and fight them.{{1}}
blocks.5: Three doors. While the first two stood open, the third could not be touched. The sword was the last way, not the first. The aim of war was not to make anyone Muslim by force; it was the end of fitnah and oppression. The Qur’an has stated this limit of war like this,
blocks.7: Fight them until fitnah ends and the religion becomes Allah’s. Then if they desist, (know that) there should be no severity against anyone other than the wrongdoers.{{1}}
blocks.8: ‘If they desist’; with these few words war stops. For the one who has stopped, there is no permission to raise a hand. Severity is only for the wrongdoer. We often pick the harshest word in the very first sentence; at home, at work, in arguments. Yet even the one into whose hand the sword was placed was told to open two doors first. Before saying the hard word, have I kept the two gentle paths open!
blocks.9: Not a Wish to Meet the Enemy
blocks.10: On one expedition, as they waited before the enemy, the sun began to decline. The Prophet {{1}} stood among the Companions and said,
blocks.12: O people, do not wish for meeting the enemy; ask Allah for safety. But when you do meet them, be steadfast. And know that Paradise is beneath the shade of swords.{{1}}
blocks.13: The one who is the bravest is the very one saying, do not wish for war. Bravery does not mean seeking out fights; it means not turning back when a fight comes. Those in whose hands power rests often look for a chance to show it. The Prophet {{1}} taught that asking for safety is itself the real asking. Let there be strength; but let there be no need for it.
blocks.14: The Woman Who Was Not Fighting
blocks.15: On one expedition, people were standing in a crowd at one place. The Prophet {{1}} sent someone, go and see what the crowd is. He came back and said, a woman lies killed. At the head of the army was Khalid ibn al-Walid (RA). The Prophet {{2}} spoke; then he sent someone to Khalid,
blocks.17: This one was not someone to fight! … Go and tell Khalid, let him not kill any woman, nor any hired labourer.{{1}}
blocks.18: The word ‘asif’ means a hired labourer. The man who has come with the army to tend camels, draw water, carry loads; no sword in his hand. The measure of the prohibition is a question: was this one fighting? To make a target of one who is not fighting is forbidden. The general prohibition on killing women and children came in dars fourteen. Here came its reason, from the Prophet’s {{1}} own mouth.{{2}}
blocks.19: In anger we too punish wholesale. A whole family for one person’s fault, a whole department for one employee’s mistake. Even on the battlefield the Prophet {{1}} told them to look separately at who had raised a hand and who had not.
blocks.20: The Question in the Dark of Night
blocks.21: At al-Abwa’ or Waddan the Prophet {{1}} was passing by Sa‘b ibn Jaththamah (RA). There a question was put to him. Sa‘b (RA) remembered the question and the answer,
blocks.23: He was asked about the settlement of the polytheists that is raided at night, in which their women and children also get hurt. He said, they too are counted among them.{{1}}
blocks.24: In the earlier scene the Prophet {{1}} was angry on seeing the slain woman. Here he said, they too are counted among them. Put side by side, the two statements seem opposite to each other. They are not opposite. The questions are different.
blocks.25: In the case of the slain woman the question was whether one may kill by making someone a target. The answer: not one who is not fighting. Sa‘b’s question is another. A raid in the darkness of night. All asleep, who is who, no way to tell. The targets were fighters. But in the same house a mother sleeps, a child sleeps. What if they are hurt in the raid? The answer: in that situation they are counted, in ruling, with their fathers. For those who were hurt unintentionally while reaching the fathers, the responsibility was not placed on the raider. Unintentionally. Everything is in this one word. Nowhere in this hadith is there permission to knowingly target a woman or a child.{{1}}
blocks.26: Al-Zuhri (may Allah have mercy on him) said at the end of the hadith, after this the Prophet {{1}} forbade the killing of women and children. The prohibition and this answer come together at one place. Not on purpose; not if recognised. If a blow lands within an unavoidable mixing, there is no fault. And if someone knowingly kills one whom it was forbidden to kill? No diyah (blood-money) or kaffarah (expiation) falls upon him; what comes is the duty of repentance (tawbah) and seeking forgiveness (istighfar).{{2}}
blocks.27: When the Prophet {{1}} himself reached any settlement at night, he waited until dawn. That event will come in dars twenty-one. Many decisions we make in half-darkness; not all the information is at hand. Then what matters is to keep the intention clear, and not to give up even the effort to avoid the harm that can be avoided.
blocks.28: The Old Man, the Worshipper and the Fruit-Bearing Tree
blocks.29: After the Prophet’s {{1}} passing, the Caliph Abu Bakr (RA) sent several armies toward Sham. The commander of one was Yazid ibn Abi Sufyan. The army set out. The commander on horseback; the Caliph was walking beside him. Yazid said, either you mount, or I get down. Abu Bakr (RA) said, you will not get down, and I will not mount; I am counting these steps in the way of Allah. Then he said,
blocks.31: On the way you will find some people who think they have shut themselves away for Allah; leave them to that for which they have shut themselves away. … And I advise you with ten things. Do not kill any woman, any child, any decrepit old man. Do not cut a fruit-bearing tree. Do not ruin an inhabited settlement. Do not slaughter any goat or camel except for the need to eat. Do not burn a beehive, nor drown it. Do not misappropriate the spoils of war. And do not be a coward.{{1}}
blocks.32: After the Prophet {{1}}, the first Caliph, the first large army. And his first words were not about how to defeat the enemy; but about whom may not be touched. A person who has shut himself away in a house of worship, a decrepit old man, a fruit-bearing tree, a beehive. In the reckoning of war these have no value; for exactly that reason they are named separately. The jurists have put the crippled and the blind in this list too. The reason is one: permission for war is because of fighting, and these are not people of fighting.{{2}}
blocks.34: Yet at the siege of Banu al-Nadir some palm trees were cut and burned on the Prophet’s {{1}} own order; the Qur’an gave permission for it too. That event is in dars seventeen. Then what is the rule? The rule is: destruction is not the aim. When the enemy makes the orchard a shield, when there is no way to break the siege except cutting trees, then permission is by the measure of need. And when victory is nearly certain, the same act is disliked; because it is needless destruction.{{2}}
blocks.35: When power comes into the hand there is a pull to finish off everything of the opponent. After a quarrel, dragging up all the old words; in business, sinking the rival completely. Even on the battlefield, the army that had been told to remember the beehive, how can its successors snatch away even someone’s last belonging!
blocks.36: Did You Split Open His Heart?
blocks.37: An expedition went toward the Huraqah branch of the Juhaynah tribe. Attack at dawn; the enemy fell back. Usamah ibn Zayd (RA) and an Ansari pursued a man. As soon as they surrounded him the man cried out, la ilaha illa Allah. The Ansari drew back his hand. Usamah (RA) thrust his spear; the man died. Usamah; the son of one dear to the Prophet {{1}}, himself dear. After returning to Madinah the matter came up before the Prophet {{2}}. Usamah (RA) himself said,
blocks.39: He said, he said la ilaha illa Allah, and you killed him? I said, O Messenger of Allah, he only said it out of fear of the weapon. He said, did you split open his heart, so that you could know whether he said it from the heart or not? He kept repeating the words before me; in the end I felt, if only I had accepted Islam today!{{1}}
blocks.40: A beloved person; yet that day love gave no concession. One question, again and again. Miqdad ibn al-Aswad (RA) once came with an even harder question,
blocks.42: O Messenger of Allah, suppose I fight one of the disbelievers; he strikes my hand with the sword and cuts one off, then takes refuge behind a tree and says, I have submitted to Allah. After he has said this, should I kill him? He said, do not kill him. … If you kill him, he will be in the position you were in before you killed him; and you will be in the position he was in before he said the words he said.{{1}}
blocks.43: Even the man whose hand was cut off is safe once he says the Kalimah. Even with the greatest excuse for revenge in hand. Just such an incident happened on another expedition. A man with a small flock of goats; seeing the Muslims, he gave the salam. They thought, he is giving salam to save his life; they killed him and took the flock. The Qur’an then said it like this,
blocks.45: O you who believe! When you travel in the way of Allah, investigate carefully. Do not say to one who offers you the salam, ‘You are not a believer,’ out of desire for the goods of worldly life. For with Allah are abundant spoils. You too were like this before. Then Allah favoured you. So investigate carefully. Surely Allah is fully aware of all that you do.{{1}}
blocks.46: ‘You too were like this before.’ One day for you too Islam was only a declaration of the mouth; and only that much was counted enough for you. We read people’s intentions very quickly. That one gave charity to show off; that one took up prayer for gain. The Prophet’s {{1}} question is as sharp today; did you split open his heart!
blocks.48: A basic principle came out of the incident of Usamah (RA). The Prophet {{1}} stated it like this,
blocks.50: Whoever prays our prayer, faces our qiblah, eats our slaughtered animal, he is the Muslim; for him is the covenant of Allah and the covenant of His Messenger. So do not betray Allah in the covenant He has given.{{1}}
blocks.51: As long as revelation was descending, sometimes from the sky itself someone’s mask would be removed. After the Prophet {{1}} that door is shut. ‘Umar (RA) therefore said,
blocks.53: In the time of the Messenger of Allah {{1}} some people were taken to account through revelation. Now revelation has stopped. Now we will take you to account by your outward deeds. Whoever shows us good, we will keep him safe, draw him near; nothing of his inner self is our concern, the reckoning of the inner is for Allah to take.{{2}}
blocks.54: The outward is in people’s hands; the inward is in Allah’s hand. When this division gets confused, a person sits down in Allah’s seat.
blocks.55: Calling One’s Own Brother a Disbeliever
blocks.56: The reverse side of this is even more frightening. The Prophet {{1}} said,
blocks.58: If anyone says to his brother, O disbeliever, then the word will surely return upon one of the two.{{1}}
blocks.59: In another hadith it says that to accuse a believer of kufr is like killing him.{{1}}
blocks.60: Takfir means the ruling that puts someone out of Islam. After it, blood, property, marriage, funeral prayer; the reckoning of everything changes. So this ruling is not for emotion, not for a party; it is for deep knowledge and careful judgment.
blocks.61: At any difference of opinion we stick labels. This one is an innovator, that one is astray, that one is outside Islam itself. A word that can come back and land on oneself needs to be weighed twice before it leaves the mouth.

footnotes.0: Sahih Muslim 1731 (Kitab al-Jihad wa al-Siyar; from Buraydah ibn al-Husayb (RA)). The full text includes the part in between about migrating (hijrah) after accepting Islam or remaining in Bedouin status, and the part about the covenant (dhimmah) and judgment concerning the people of fortresses (the latter part is in the footnote to the section ‘The Line Between Strategy and Deception’ in this dars). Sunan Abi Dawud 2613 (al-Albani: sahih). The Arabic text of the hadith has the words ‘mina al-mushrikin’ (from among the polytheists); the quotation in the dars is a translation of just that. In Hanafi fiqh, among these three options, jizyah may be taken from the People of the Book (Arab or non-Arab), fire-worshippers and non-Arab polytheists; not from Arab polytheists, for whom it is either Islam or the sword (al-Kasani, Bada’i‘ al-Sana’i‘, Kitab al-Siyar, vol. 9, pp. 428, 433; evidence Tawbah 9:5 and 9:29).
footnotes.1: Tawdih al-Qur’an, vol. 1, Surah al-Baqarah 2:193, p. 120 (Taqi ‘Uthmani; checked against the rendered printed page). Note 123: in the Shari‘ah the aim of jihad is not to force anyone to accept Islam; in the ordinary situation, if anyone wants to remain firm in kufr, they can stay by showing respect for the law of the Islamic state through the jizyah (the ruling for the Arabian Peninsula is different).
footnotes.2: Sahih al-Bukhari 2965–2966, 3024–3025; Sahih Muslim 1742 (from ‘Abdullah ibn Abi Awfa (RA)). At the end of the hadith the Prophet’s {{1}} du‘a: ‘O Allah, Revealer of the Book, Mover of the clouds, Defeater of the combined armies, defeat them, help us.’
footnotes.3: Sunan Abi Dawud 2669 (from Rabah ibn al-Rabi‘ al-Usayyidi (RA), through his grandson ‘Umar ibn al-Murraqqi‘); al-Albani: hasan sahih; Silsilah Sahihah 701 (chain sahih); Sahih Ibn Hibban 4791 (Shu‘ayb al-Arna’ut: chain sahih). ‘Asif’ (‘asif) = a hired labourer or servant, who does not take part in the fighting.
footnotes.4: Sahih al-Bukhari 3014–3015 (from Ibn ‘Umar (RA); the prohibition of killing women and children on seeing the slain woman), quoted in dars 14.
footnotes.5: Sahih al-Bukhari 3012; Sahih Muslim 1745; Sunan Abi Dawud 2672; Musnad Ahmad 16426 (from Sa‘b ibn Jaththamah (RA); ‘the Prophet {{1}} passed by me at al-Abwa’ or Waddan; he was asked…’). In the text of al-Bukhari the questioner has no name (‘su’ila’, he was asked); in the text of Musnad Ahmad Sa‘b himself asked.
footnotes.6: Ibn Hajar, Fath al-Bari, commentary on 3012 (Salafiyyah edition, Kitab al-Jihad; PDF no. 07 in your folder, printed pp. 147–148): ‘hum minhum’ means ‘in that situation in terms of ruling’; the intention is not to indicate permission to kill women and children by targeting them (‘bi-tariq al-qasd’). The intention is: if there is no way to reach the fathers without trampling over them, and they get hurt because of being mixed in, then that is permissible. ‘Bayat’ means a night raid in such a way that individuals cannot be told apart. ‘Amr ibn Dinar understood the words as ‘they are with their fathers’ (Sunan Abi Dawud 2672). The statement ‘after this the Prophet {{1}} forbade the killing of women and children’ is al-Zuhri’s, not the Prophet’s {{2}} own words; as for the words ‘day of Hunayn’ added in Ibn Hibban’s narration, Ibn Hajar called it an addition by the narrator (‘mudraj’), and called the hadith of Rabah ibn al-Rabi‘ (Abu Dawud 2669) a supporter of this later prohibition. Some have taken Sa‘b’s hadith as abrogated on the basis of al-Zuhri’s statement; al-Hazimi said the opposite, that Sa‘b’s hadith itself abrogated the prohibition hadiths, which Ibn Hajar called ‘gharib’. Most scholars have reconciled the two: this is the view of al-Shafi‘i and the jurists of Kufah. The view of Malik and al-Awza‘i is stricter still: even if they are used as a shield, women and children may not be targeted.
footnotes.7: Al-Kasani, Bada’i‘ al-Sana’i‘, Kitab al-Siyar (vol. 9; PDF no. 10 in the folder): p. 393: ‘there is no harm in a surprise night raid and bayat’ (‘wa la ba’sa bi-l-bayat’). p. 400: if one (knowingly) kills any of those whose killing is not lawful, there is no diyah or kaffarah, only tawbah and istighfar; because the legal value of an unbeliever’s blood is not fixed without aman (safe-conduct). Editorial note on p. 398: that the killing of women and children is forbidden if they do not fight, the jurists agree. The Prophet’s {{1}} arriving at night and waiting until dawn: Sahih al-Bukhari 610 (dars 21).
footnotes.8: Muwatta’ Imam Malik, Kitab al-Jihad, Bab al-Nahy ‘an Qatl al-Nisa’ wa al-Wildan, no. 982 (from Yahya ibn Sa‘id, without a connected chain up to Abu Bakr (RA); the dialogue of walking is in the wording ‘za‘amu’, that is, ‘people say’). Shu‘ayb al-Arna’ut, Takhrij Sharh al-Sunnah 2696: ‘the narrators are trustworthy, but the chain is broken (munqati‘)’; al-Bayhaqi, Ma‘rifat al-Sunan 18075–18078: through several broken chains; Ibn Kathir, Irshad al-Faqih 2/320: ‘narrated from Abu Bakr (RA) through many chains’. This is not a hadith of the Prophet {{1}}, it is the Caliph’s advice (athar); the jurists accepted it because its content is consistent with the sahih hadiths (Abu Dawud 2669; Bukhari 3014–3015). The reading ‘nahlan’ (bees) is the Muwatta’s (the original text checked); in some narrations, including in Ibn Kathir’s quotation, ‘nakhlan’ (palm trees). The part in the middle that was omitted (about a group of fighters with the middle of the head shaved) is outside the subject of the dars.
footnotes.9: Al-Kasani, Bada’i‘ al-Sana’i‘ (Dar al-Kutub al-‘Ilmiyyah, edited by ‘Ali Mu‘awwad and ‘Adil ‘Abd al-Mawjud), Kitab al-Siyar, ‘Fasl fi Bayan Man Yahillu Qatluhu wa Man la Yahillu’, pp. 398–400: during fighting it is not lawful to kill women, children, decrepit old men, the crippled, those paralysed on one side, the blind, those with hands and feet cut off, the insane, monks in places of worship, hermits on mountains, and worshippers who stay in their homes with doors closed; ‘because these are not people of fighting’ (‘li’anna ha’ula’i laysu min ahl al-qital’). Principle: one who is a person of fighting, killing him is lawful; one who is not, only when he actually fights, or takes part in the fighting by giving counsel, obedience and incitement; even if a woman or child (at Hunayn the old Duraid ibn al-Simmah, whose counsel alone was of use, was killed, the Prophet {{1}} did not object).
footnotes.10: Surah al-Hashr 59:5; Sahih al-Bukhari 4031 (cutting and burning the palm trees of Banu al-Nadir), detailed in dars 17. Al-Kasani, Bada’i‘ al-Sana’i‘ (Dar al-Kutub al-‘Ilmiyyah, edited by ‘Ali Mu‘awwad and ‘Adil ‘Abd al-Mawjud), Kitab al-Siyar, pp. 393–394: there is no harm in cutting the enemy’s fruit-bearing and fruitless trees, destroying crops, burning or flooding fortresses, the evidence Hashr 59:5 and 59:2. But when victory is nearly certain it is makruh, because it is destruction beyond need: Ibn al-Humam, Fath al-Qadir (commentary on al-Hidayah), quoted in the note on the same page of Bada’i‘ al-Sana’i‘. ‘Ali Muhammad al-Sallabi, The Prophet’s Life of War (Bengali), p. 274 (‘Destroying the Enemy’s Wealth and Crops’).
footnotes.11: Sahih Muslim 96; Sahih al-Bukhari 4269, 6872 (from Usamah ibn Zayd (RA); the Huraqah expedition). ‘If only I had accepted Islam today’ means: then accepting Islam would have wiped out all previous sins, this mistake too (the Bukhari text: ‘if only I had not been Muslim before today’). Usamah is the son of Zayd ibn Harithah, the Prophet’s {{1}} freed slave and adopted son.
footnotes.12: Sahih al-Bukhari 4019; Sahih Muslim 95 (from Miqdad ibn al-Aswad (RA)); Sunan Abi Dawud 2644 (al-Albani: sahih).
footnotes.13: Tawdih al-Qur’an, vol. 1, Surah al-Nisa’ 4:94, pp. 270–271. Occasion of revelation: Sahih al-Bukhari 4591; Sahih Muslim 3025 (Ibn ‘Abbas (RA): the man with the flock of goats gave the salam, yet he was killed and the flock taken, then the verse was revealed). Tawdih note 59: if someone accepts Islam before us we shall consider them Muslim, the state of the heart is with Allah; note 60: ‘you too were like this before’, that is, there was no proof of your being Muslim other than a verbal declaration.
footnotes.14: Sahih al-Bukhari 391 (from Anas ibn Malik (RA)); in the same sense 393.
footnotes.15: Sahih al-Bukhari 2641 (from ‘Umar ibn al-Khattab (RA)). The end of the text: ‘And whoever shows us evil, we shall not consider him safe, nor trust him, even if he says that his inside is good.’
footnotes.17: Sahih al-Bukhari 6105, 6652 (from Thabit ibn al-Dahhak (RA)): ‘To accuse a believer of kufr is like killing him.’

quiz.q: What did the Prophet ﷺ tell the army’s commander to call the enemy to first?
o: To the jizyah
To Islam
To a truce
To aman (safe-conduct)
quiz.e: The first door is Islam, then jizyah, then fighting (Sahih Muslim 1731).

quiz.q: Which Companion remembered the instruction the Prophet ﷺ gave to the commander?
o: al-Nu‘man ibn Muqarrin (RA)
Abu Usayd al-Sa‘idi (RA)
Buraydah ibn al-Husayb (RA)
Sa‘b ibn Jaththamah al-Laythi (RA)
quiz.e: Sahih Muslim 1731, from Buraydah (RA).

quiz.q: In the hadith ‘do not wish to meet the enemy’, where is Paradise said to be?
o: Beneath the feet of mothers
In the drops of the martyr’s blood
In the field of shooting arrows
Beneath the shade of swords
quiz.e: ‘Know that Paradise is beneath the shade of swords’ (Sahih al-Bukhari 2966).

quiz.q: What can be understood about the aim of war from the ‘three doors’?
o: The aim is to annihilate the enemy completely
Gaining spoils is the main aim
Forcing people to become Muslim is not the aim
Taking revenge is the real aim
quiz.e: That the jizyah door is open proves that the aim is the end of fitnah and oppression (Tawdih, note on 2:193).

quiz.q: ‘Do not wish to meet the enemy’ and ‘be steadfast when you meet them’; together, what definition of bravery do they make?
o: Always being eager for fighting
Proposing a truce on seeing the enemy
Avoiding the field for safety
Not seeking fights, not turning back if one comes
quiz.e: Asking for safety is the real asking; but steadfastness when the fight comes.

quiz.q: What does the lesson of the ‘three doors’ say when there is a difference of opinion at the office?
o: Keep the gentle paths open before harsh words
Say the harshest word at the very start
Quietly withdraw when there is a difference
Report directly to the authority
quiz.e: Even the swordsman was told to open two doors first.

quiz.q: On seeing the slain woman, whom did the Prophet ﷺ send word to Khalid (RA) not to kill?
o: Women and hired labourers
The old and worshippers
Women and blind people equally
The crippled and children
quiz.e: ‘Tell Khalid, let him not kill any woman, nor any hired labourer’ (Abu Dawud 2669).

quiz.q: What does the word ‘asif’ mean?
o: A decrepit old man
A hired labourer
A person engaged in worship
An adviser in war
quiz.e: ‘Asif: a hired labourer who comes with the army, with no sword in his hand.

quiz.q: From the statement ‘This one was not someone to fight!’, what is the measure of the prohibition on killing?
o: Whether the person is taking part in the fighting
Which tribe the person belongs to
Whether the person is from the Muslims’ enemy side
Whether the person has wealth
quiz.e: In Hanafi fiqh too the basis of permission to kill is fighting (al-hirab).

quiz.q: Punishing a whole department for one employee’s mistake goes against which lesson?
o: Saving the arrows
Looking separately at who has raised a hand
News first, then the foot
What my man gives as word is my word
quiz.e: Seeing the slain woman, the Prophet ﷺ separated fighter from non-fighter.

quiz.q: Where was the question about the night raid asked?
o: On the road to Badr at Harrat al-Wabarah
At Wadi al-Qura
At al-Abwa’ or Waddan
On the Huraqah expedition
quiz.e: Sa‘b (RA) said that the Prophet ﷺ was passing by him at al-Abwa’ or Waddan (Sahih al-Bukhari 3012).

quiz.q: How do the hadith of the slain woman and Sa‘b’s hadith ‘they too are counted among them’ fit together?
o: Making them a target is forbidden, hurt from unintended mixing is different
Sa‘b’s hadith gives a general permission to kill women and children
The hadith of the slain woman applies only to one particular expedition
The contradiction between the two remains, so one has to be taken as abrogated
quiz.e: The two questions are different: killing by targeting, and a blow landing in unavoidable mixing in a night raid (Ibn Hajar).

quiz.q: ‘They too are counted among them’; this answer is about what kind of harm?
o: Knowingly and deliberately targeting women and children
Hurt that lands unintentionally in the dark
Treatment of captive women
Cutting the enemy’s fruit-bearing trees
quiz.e: The prohibition on intentional killing is separate; the question is about harm that cannot be avoided.

quiz.q: If one has to make a big decision with incomplete information, what is the dars’s lesson?
o: Do nothing until all the information is had
Whatever harm results, place the responsibility fully on others
Keep the intention clear and avoid the harm that can be avoided
Bring quick results by any means
quiz.e: The lesson of the question in the dark of night.

quiz.q: Beside which commander was Abu Bakr (RA) walking on the road to Sham?
o: Khalid ibn al-Walid
Mu‘awiyah ibn Abi Sufyan
Usamah ibn Zayd
Yazid ibn Abi Sufyan
quiz.e: Commander on horse, Caliph on foot; when Yazid wanted to get down he spoke of counting the steps in Allah’s way.

quiz.q: What does Abu Bakr’s (RA) advice forbid burning or drowning?
o: A beehive
The enemy’s fortress
An inhabited settlement
The spoils of war
quiz.e: ‘Do not burn a beehive, nor drown it.’

quiz.q: What is the status of Abu Bakr’s (RA) advice?
o: A connected hadith of the Prophet ﷺ
A direct explanation of a Qur’anic verse
The Caliph’s advice, with a broken chain
A sahih marfu‘ narration of al-Bukhari
quiz.e: In the Muwatta’ with a broken chain; its content is consistent with sahih hadiths.

quiz.q: The cutting of Banu al-Nadir’s palm trees and ‘do not cut a fruit-bearing tree’; what is the resolution?
o: The later command abrogated the earlier
Only in the Caliph’s time did tree-cutting become forbidden
Both are part of a general permission
Permission when needed, not without need
quiz.e: When victory is nearly certain, cutting trees is makruh; because it is needless destruction (al-Hidayah).

quiz.q: Against the tendency to sink a rival completely in business, which picture stands opposite?
o: The man who said the Kalimah behind a tree
That chief of Yamamah tied to the mosque pillar
The night raid on a settlement in the dark
Remembering the beehive even on a war march
quiz.e: Not snatching away anyone’s last possession even when power is in hand.

quiz.q: Which expedition was Usamah’s (RA) incident from?
o: The expedition of the Najd cavalry
The Huraqah expedition of Juhaynah
The expedition on the road to Badr
The expedition of Wadi al-Qura

quiz.q: Who asked about the man who said the Kalimah after his hand was cut off?
o: Usamah ibn Zayd (RA)
Sa‘b ibn Jaththamah (RA)
Miqdad ibn al-Aswad (RA)
Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman (RA)

quiz.q: In the occasion of revelation of verse 94 of Surah al-Nisa’, what had the man done?
o: Said the Kalimah
Hid behind a tree
Wanted to pay the jizyah
Gave the salam

quiz.q: What is the main lesson of the question ‘Did you split open his heart?’
o: Judgment of the heart is not in people’s hands
The Kalimah has no value in war
A Kalimah said out of fear of weapons is not acceptable
A dear one’s mistake should be forgiven

quiz.q: In Miqdad’s question, what is the significance of ‘you will go to his position’?
o: Gaining the right to take revenge for the cut hand
By killing a safe Muslim one’s own blood becomes claimable

o: You too were prisoners of war before

o: Did you split open his heart?

o: Because there are no more hypocrites
As a new policy of the caliphate
Because the number of judges is small
Because revelation has stopped
quiz.e: In the Prophet’s ﷺ time some people were taken through revelation; now revelation has stopped.

quiz.q: Which hadith is important to remember before declaring someone ‘outside Islam’ over a difference of opinion?
o: The Muslims’ covenant is one, even an ordinary person can give it
The word ‘disbeliever’ returns upon one of the two

Strength is shooting arrows

porbos.title: Treatment of Prisoners • Ghanimah, Fay’ and a Cloak • Umm Hani’s Refuge • Covenants and Their Breach

blocks.1: The seventy prisoners of Badr, the advice about ransom, and after that Allah’s warning; all this was told in dars fifteen.{{1}}
blocks.2: Later the ruling was settled. The Qur’an has said it like this,
blocks.4: Finally, when you have crushed their strength, then bind them firmly. Then, if you wish, release them, either out of grace or by taking ransom.{{1}}
blocks.5: Releasing out of grace, or taking ransom. Which path is to be taken, the ruler will decide, looking at the welfare of the Muslims.
blocks.7: At the field of Badr this question came up as a hard one. ‘Abd al-Rahman ibn ‘Awf (RA) was taking Umayyah ibn Khalaf and his son as prisoners. In Makkah this very Umayyah used to lay Bilal (RA) down on the hot sand. Bilal (RA) saw him. He went to the gathering of the Ansar and called out. A group of the Ansar came running. ‘Abd al-Rahman (RA) threw himself over the prisoner; they swung their swords from beneath him and killed Umayyah.{{1}}
blocks.8: Umayyah was not a woman, not a child. At Badr he had come as part of Quraysh’s army, as a fighter. A fighter, even when captured, does not get safety of life. The fate of a prisoner is decided by the imam; killing, enslaving, or making him a dhimmi (a protected subject). At Badr itself the Prophet {{1}} had ordered the killing of ‘Uqbah ibn Abi Mu‘ayt and al-Nadr ibn al-Harith. But that day the decision was not in the imam’s hands. A group of the Ansar killed ‘Abd al-Rahman’s prisoner. The rule of fiqh is clear here. No one should kill another’s prisoner, because by the capture a special right of the captor arises over the prisoner. And the better course is to take him to the imam, so that he makes the decision.{{2}}
blocks.9: The incident is narrated in the words of an eyewitness, as a scene of one night. There is no verdict of the Prophet {{1}} in it. So this is not a rule, it is an event. The memory of the persecution in Makkah, seeing a known enemy, called a ‘head of kufr’, in captivity; the anger was truly there that day. Yet the rule is for the very moment of anger: the decision about a prisoner is in the imam’s hands.
blocks.10: The Chief Tied to the Mosque Pillar
blocks.11: A cavalry party went toward Najd. They brought back a man of Banu Hanifah; the chief of Yamamah, Thumamah ibn Uthal. He was tied to one of the pillars of the Prophet’s Mosque. The Prophet {{1}} came out and asked, Thumamah, what do you have? Thumamah said,
blocks.13: I have something good, O Muhammad. If you kill, you will kill one whose blood has a claimant. If you show favour, you will show favour to one who is grateful. And if you want wealth, ask for as much as you wish.{{1}}
blocks.14: The next day the same question, the same answer. The day after too. For three days he stayed tied inside the mosque. On the third day the Prophet {{1}} said, release Thumamah. No ransom, no condition. Thumamah went to a date grove near the mosque, bathed, came back, entered the mosque and recited the Kalimah. Then he said,
blocks.16: O Muhammad, by Allah, there was no face on the earth more hateful to me than your face; today your face is dearer to me than all faces. By Allah, there was no religion more hateful to me than your religion; today your religion is the dearest religion to me. By Allah, there was no city more hateful to me than your city; today your city is the dearest city to me.{{1}}
blocks.17: When he went to Makkah to perform ‘umrah, someone said, you have become an apostate! Thumamah (RA) said, no; I have accepted Islam with Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah {{1}}. By Allah, not even a grain of wheat will come to you from Yamamah until the Prophet {{2}} gives permission. The one who a few days earlier had been a prisoner tied to a pillar was now standing blocking Makkah’s bread route.
blocks.18: To release the one whom one has full right to punish; there are few greater invitations than this. When a subordinate makes a mistake and falls into our grasp, we often take the full payback. Yet at the very moment of forgiving, sometimes an enemy becomes a friend.
blocks.20: For the communities of earlier prophets the wealth won in war was not lawful. The Prophet {{1}} said,
blocks.22: I have been given five things which were not given to anyone before me. … Spoils of war have been made lawful for me, which were not lawful for anyone before me.{{1}}
blocks.23: But being lawful does not mean plunder. The spoils will be gathered in one place. One-fifth goes to the heads set by Allah and His Messenger; the rest is divided among the fighters. And wealth that comes into the hand without fighting is called fay’. The wealth of Banu al-Nadir was of that kind. ‘Umar (RA) said,
blocks.25: The wealth of Banu al-Nadir was that fay’ which Allah gave to His Messenger, for which the Muslims did not have to run horses or camels. So it was reserved for the Messenger of Allah {{1}}. He would keep from it the expenses of his family for a year; the rest he would spend on weapons and horses, as preparation in the way of Allah.{{2}}
blocks.26: Of the wealth that is entirely in his own hand, one year’s provision for his own household; the rest for the defence of the Ummah.
blocks.27: The Cloak That Burns With Fire
blocks.28: Khaybar was conquered. No gold or silver was found; what was found was cattle, camels, goods and orchards. Then the army moved toward Wadi al-Qura. With the Prophet {{1}} was a slave named Mid‘am; someone had given him to him as a gift. At Wadi al-Qura he was unloading the Prophet’s {{2}} saddle. Suddenly from somewhere an arrow came and struck; he died right there. The people said, may Paradise be blessed for him! The Prophet {{3}} said,
blocks.30: Never! By the One in whose hand is my soul, the cloak that he took from the spoils on the day of Khaybar, which had not fallen to his share in the distribution, is burning upon him as fire.{{1}}
blocks.31: Hearing this, one man brought one or two shoe-laces. The Prophet {{1}} said, one lace of fire, or two laces of fire. A cloak, a shoe-lace. Not even death on the battlefield could cover it. The distribution of Hunayn’s spoils and the Ansar’s hurt feelings will come in dars twenty-three.{{2}}
blocks.32: Office paper, the institution’s pen, two coins from an organisation’s fund; what is that. That cloak of Khaybar was nothing much either. Yet that very thing was burning as fire.
blocks.34: The day of the conquest of Makkah. ‘Ali’s (RA) sister Umm Hani (RA) had given shelter in her house to a polytheist of her in-laws’ family. ‘Ali (RA) was saying, I will kill him for sure. Umm Hani (RA) went to the Prophet {{1}}. He was bathing at that time; his daughter Fatimah (RA) had screened him with a cloth. She greeted him with salam. The Prophet {{2}} asked, who is it? She said, I am Umm Hani, daughter of Abu Talib. He said, welcome, Umm Hani. After bathing he wrapped one cloth around himself and prayed eight rak‘ahs. When the prayer was over Umm Hani (RA) said, O Messenger of Allah, my mother’s son ‘Ali says he will kill a man whom I have given shelter; so-and-so son of Hubayrah. The Prophet {{3}} said,
blocks.36: Umm Hani, whom you have given shelter, we too have given shelter.{{1}}
blocks.37: ‘Ali, hero of the victorious army; a woman the giver of shelter. The verdict went in favour of the woman’s word. Behind this was a general principle, which the Prophet {{1}} had already stated,
blocks.39: The covenant of the Muslims is one; even the most ordinary of them can give it. Whoever breaks the covenant given by any Muslim, upon him is the curse of Allah, of the angels and of all people.{{1}}
blocks.40: When a Muslim gives someone security, the whole Ummah takes on responsibility for that word.{{1}}
blocks.41: When someone of the household gives a promise to someone, we often say, he gave the promise, I did not. The Prophet {{1}} taught the opposite. My man gave a promise means I myself gave a promise.
blocks.43: Before Badr, Hudhayfah (RA) and his father were caught by Quraysh and promised not to enter the fighting. The Prophet {{1}} told them to keep that promise, even on a day like Badr; that event is in dars fifteen.{{2}}
blocks.44: As long as the covenant is there, it is to be kept. And even if the fear of treachery from the enemy’s side appears, the covenant may not be broken secretly. The Qur’an has said it like this,
blocks.46: If you fear treachery from any people, then cast the covenant straight back at them. Remember, Allah does not like those who break faith.{{1}}
blocks.47: ‘Cast it straight back at them’; that is, first announce openly that the covenant is no more. No step before announcing. And regarding those who have kept the covenant, the instruction is even clearer. The Qur’an has said it like this,
blocks.49: But (O Muslims!) those polytheists with whom you made a covenant and who afterwards did not fail you in keeping the covenant, nor aided anyone against you, complete the covenant with them to the end of its term. Surely Allah loves those who are cautious.{{1}}
blocks.50: The tribe whose covenant had nine more months left was given the full nine months.
blocks.52: A matter long after the Prophet {{1}}. A fixed-term treaty between Mu‘awiyah (RA) and the Romans. Before the term ran out he was advancing with an army toward their land, so that they could attack the moment the term ended. Suddenly a horseman came running, takbir on his lips; Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar! Wafa’, not ghadr; keeping the promise, not betrayal! He was ‘Amr ibn ‘Abasah (RA). Mu‘awiyah (RA) called him and asked the reason. He said, I heard the Messenger of Allah {{2}} say,
blocks.54: If anyone has a covenant with a people, until its term expires he should neither tighten any knot of the covenant nor loosen it; or he should announce to them on equal terms that there is no covenant.{{1}}
blocks.55: Mu‘awiyah (RA) turned back with the army. Even gathering troops on the border within the term was counted as a breach of the covenant. And upon hearing one hadith a whole army turned back. What can be the consequence of breaking a covenant was seen in the incident of Banu Qurayzah. At the hardest moment of the Trench they broke the pact; the judgment was given by Sa‘d ibn Mu‘adh (RA). That event is in dars eighteen.{{1}}
blocks.56: And if the enemy wants peace? The Qur’an has said it like this,
blocks.58: And if they incline toward peace, then you too incline toward it and put your trust in Allah. Surely He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.{{1}}
blocks.59: The Line Between Strategy and Deception
blocks.60: Keeping the limits does not mean giving up strategy. The Prophet {{1}} himself said, in two small words,
blocks.63: Confusing the enemy, hiding one’s own plan; these are allowed in war. But breaking a word given by word is not strategy; it is betrayal. How carefully the Prophet {{1}} drew this line, there is a sample in that very instruction to the commander. When the people of a fortress asked for the covenant of Allah and His Messenger, the commander was told, give your own covenant and your companions’; because failing to keep a covenant you yourselves gave is lighter than failing to keep the covenant of Allah and His Messenger.{{2}}
blocks.64: So that Allah’s name does not get tangled with any broken word; this much caution. Firming up an arrangement secretly with a new supplier before the contract term ends; promising it to someone else without telling the tenant. In the eyes of the law perhaps there is no fault. But that call of ‘Amr ibn ‘Abasah says the same thing even today; wafa’, not ghadr.

footnotes.0: The prisoners of Badr and ransom: Sahih Muslim 1763; Surah al-Anfal 8:67–69 (detailed in dars 15).
footnotes.1: Tawdih al-Qur’an, vol. 3, Surah Muhammad 47:4 (part), p. 350. Note 2 (pp. 350–351): at present it is permissible for a Muslim ruler to release without ransom out of grace, or to release for ransom or exchange of prisoners; but this discretion applies only when there is no treaty with the enemy side on the matter of prisoners of war; if there is a treaty, acting according to it is obligatory. The zahir al-riwayah of the Hanafi school is different: al-Kasani, Bada’i‘ al-Sana’i‘ (Dar al-Kutub al-‘Ilmiyyah, edited by ‘Ali Mu‘awwad and ‘Adil ‘Abd al-Mawjud), Kitab al-Siyar, pp. 480–485: the ruler may kill the prisoner, enslave him, or release him as a dhimmi; releasing out of unconditional grace is not permissible, and release for money is not permitted in the zahir al-riwayah either (Imam Muhammad: an old man with no hope of having children may be released for money); release in exchange for a Muslim prisoner is not permitted in the view of Imam Abu Hanifah, permitted in the view of Imam Abu Yusuf and Imam Muhammad. Al-Kasani reports that some have called 47:4 abrogated by Tawbah 9:5, or have said it applies to the People of the Book, as at Khaybar. In al-Siyar al-Kabir it is said that if the Muslims have need, there is no harm in release for money (quoted in the note on the same page). Tormenting a prisoner with hunger and thirst is forbidden (p. 485).
footnotes.2: Sahih al-Bukhari 2301 (from ‘Abd al-Rahman ibn ‘Awf (RA)): the earlier written agreement with Umayyah (to protect family and property), taking him toward the mountain on the day of Badr when people slept to make him safe, Bilal’s call ‘Umayyah ibn Khalaf, if he lives I shall not live’, ‘a group of the Ansar went out with him’, and ‘they swung their swords from beneath me and killed him’. This narration speaks only of a group of the Ansar as the strikers; there is no mention of Bilal’s own hand striking. There is no verdict or comment of the Prophet {{1}} in this narration. The Prophet’s {{2}} advance word about Umayyah: Sahih al-Bukhari 3632, 3950 (from Sa‘d ibn Mu‘adh (RA), in dars 15). Umayyah’s persecution of Bilal is Sirah-based (Ibn Ishaq; dars 7 and 15).
footnotes.3: Al-Kasani, Bada’i‘ al-Sana’i‘, Kitab al-Siyar (vol. 9): pp. 480–481: the imam chooses among prisoners: killing, enslaving, or releasing them as dhimmis; the Prophet {{1}} on the day of Badr ordered the killing of ‘Uqbah ibn Abi Mu‘ayt and al-Nadr ibn al-Harith (p. 481). p. 485: no one should kill another’s prisoner (‘asira sahibihi’), because by capture a special right of the captor arises over the prisoner; and the better course is to take the prisoner to the imam, because the rights of all the ghazis are bound up with the prisoner, so the decision is the imam’s. This is a basic principle of fiqh; the connection of the principle with Umayyah’s incident is the dars’s own, al-Kasani did not name the incident.
footnotes.4: Sahih al-Bukhari 4372, 2422; Sahih Muslim 1764 (from Abu Hurayrah (RA)). Thumamah ibn Uthal of Banu Hanifah, chief of Yamamah.
footnotes.5: Sahih al-Bukhari 4372; Sahih Muslim 1764 (from Abu Hurayrah (RA); the question ‘you have become an apostate’ in Makkah and the announcement of stopping Yamamah’s wheat are in the same hadith too).
footnotes.6: Sahih al-Bukhari 335 (from Jabir ibn ‘Abdillah (RA)); Sahih Muslim 521.
footnotes.7: Sahih al-Bukhari 2904 (from ‘Umar ibn al-Khattab (RA); through Malik ibn Aws). ‘Kura‘’ (al-kura‘) = horses and other mounts.
footnotes.8: Sahih al-Bukhari 4234; Sunan Abi Dawud 2711 (from Abu Hurayrah (RA)). The slave’s name is Mid‘am.
footnotes.9: Surah al-Anfal 8:41 (one-fifth of the spoils). The spoils of Hunayn and the speech at al-Ji‘ranah are, according to the plan, the subject of dars 23.
footnotes.10: Sahih al-Bukhari 357, 3171, 6158; Sahih Muslim 336 (from Umm Hani (RA); through Abu Murrah). The event was at the time of duha on the day of the conquest of Makkah.
footnotes.11: Sahih al-Bukhari 3179, 6755; Sahih Muslim 1370 (the hadith of the written page that was with ‘Ali (RA)).
footnotes.12: Al-Kasani, Bada’i‘ al-Sana’i‘ (Dar al-Kutub al-‘Ilmiyyah, edited by ‘Ali Mu‘awwad and ‘Adil ‘Abd al-Mawjud), Kitab al-Siyar, pp. 411–417: the pillar of aman is a word indicating security; a woman’s aman is valid (the hadith of Umm Hani (RA); Zaynab (RA) had given aman to Abu al-‘As, the Prophet {{1}} upheld it); a single Muslim’s aman is also valid, the evidence ‘even the most ordinary of them can give it’. Aman is not a binding contract; the ruler, if he sees benefit, may break it, but he will announce first, so that there is no betrayal (pp. 416–417). ‘Ali Muhammad al-Sallabi, The Prophet’s Life of War (Bengali), p. 495.
footnotes.13: Sahih Muslim 1787 (from Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman (RA): ‘we shall keep the pledge made with them, and seek Allah’s help against them’), quoted in dars 15.
footnotes.14: Tawdih al-Qur’an, vol. 1, Surah al-Anfal 8:58, p. 507. Note 40 (pp. 507–508): if there is fear of the enemy side’s breach of faith, the cancellation of the covenant must be clearly announced; taking a step against the covenant without first announcing is tantamount to breaking the covenant, which Allah does not like.
footnotes.15: Tawdih al-Qur’an, vol. 1, Surah al-Tawbah 9:4, p. 522. Note 1 (pp. 520–521), the fourth category: those with whom there was a covenant for a fixed term and who did not break it, are given the full term; the covenant of Banu Damrah and Banu Mudlij, branches of Banu Kinanah, had nine months left, so they were given nine months.
footnotes.16: Sunan Abi Dawud 2759 (Shu‘ayb al-Arna’ut and al-Albani: sahih); Jami‘ al-Tirmidhi 1580 (al-Tirmidhi: hasan sahih) (Sulaym ibn ‘Amir ← ‘Amr ibn ‘Abasah (RA)).
footnotes.17: The breach of covenant by Banu Qurayzah and Sa‘d (RA)’s judgment: Sahih al-Bukhari 3043, 4121; Sahih Muslim 1768 (detailed in dars 18).
footnotes.18: Tawdih al-Qur’an, vol. 1, Surah al-Anfal 8:61, p. 509. Note 44: this verse has permitted peace with the enemy; but the terms must be such that the Muslims’ interests are protected.
footnotes.19: Sahih al-Bukhari 3030; Sahih Muslim 1739 (from Jabir ibn ‘Abdillah (RA)).
footnotes.20: The end part of Sahih Muslim 1731 (from Buraydah (RA)): ‘fa-innakum an tukhfiru dhimamakum … ahwan’ (for you to break your own covenants … is lighter).

quiz.q: According to the narration of the incident, who killed Umayyah ibn Khalaf?
o: A group of the Ansar, at Bilal’s call
‘Abd al-Rahman ibn ‘Awf (RA) himself
The army of Khalid ibn al-Walid (RA)
Usamah ibn Zayd (RA) and an Ansari
quiz.e: Bilal brought the Ansar; they swung swords from beneath ‘Abd al-Rahman and killed him (Bukhari 2301).

quiz.q: Of which region was Thumamah ibn Uthal chief?
o: Tihamah
Yamamah
Khaybar
Wadi al-Qura
quiz.e: A man of Banu Hanifah, chief of Yamamah.

quiz.q: What did Thumamah (RA) announce he would stop from reaching Makkah?
o: Khaybar dates
Tihamah camels
Yamamah wheat
Najd horses
quiz.e: Not even a grain of wheat will come until the Prophet ﷺ gives permission.

quiz.q: What is the fiqh rule al-Kasani gives about killing another’s prisoner?
o: Anyone may kill if they wish
It should not be done; taking him to the imam is better
He can never be released without ransom
Killing a prisoner is haram in every situation
quiz.e: By capture a special right of the captor arises over the prisoner; the decision is the imam’s (al-Kasani, p. 485).

quiz.q: According to Surah Muhammad 47:4, what are the ways of releasing a prisoner?
o: By grace or by taking ransom
Only by taking ransom
Only through prisoner exchange
Only on condition of accepting Islam
quiz.e: ‘Then, if you wish, release them, either out of grace or by taking ransom.’

quiz.q: What ruling is exemplified in the story of Thumamah’s (RA) Islam?
o: Releasing the prisoner after taking ransom money
Release out of grace without ransom
A prisoner-exchange agreement
Release on the condition of jizyah
quiz.e: On the third day ‘release Thumamah’; no ransom, no condition.

quiz.q: When a subordinate makes a mistake and falls into one’s grasp, what does Thumamah’s story teach?
o: Taking the full payback when one has the chance is justice
Leaving the matter in others’ hands and staying away
At the moment of forgiving even an enemy can become a friend
Never releasing without ransom
quiz.e: Within three days hatred had turned to love.

quiz.q: From Banu al-Nadir’s fay’, after keeping the year’s expenses, where did the Prophet ﷺ spend the rest?
o: On the construction of mosques
On the Ansar’s share
On prisoners’ ransoms
On weapons and horses
quiz.e: ‘Umar (RA): the rest on weapons and horses, as preparation in the way of Allah (Bukhari 2904).

quiz.q: Where did Mid‘am die, struck by an arrow?
o: At Wadi al-Qura
In a fortress of Khaybar
At Harrat al-Wabarah on the road to Badr
At al-Abwa’
quiz.e: After Khaybar, at Wadi al-Qura, while unloading the saddle (Bukhari 4234).

quiz.q: Which ruling on spoils does Mid‘am’s cloak incident make clear?
o: Spoils were not lawful for earlier ummahs
Fay’ is reserved only for the Prophet ﷺ
Taking anything before distribution is misappropriation
A horseman gets a larger share
quiz.e: ‘Which had not fallen to his share in the distribution’; that very thing was burning as fire.

quiz.q: Which incident warns about taking the institution’s pen and paper for one’s own work?
o: Overturning a boiling pot
The spending of Banu al-Nadir’s fay’
Selling mixed dates for dirhams
The cloak of Khaybar and the shoe-lace
quiz.e: ‘One lace of fire, or two laces of fire.’

quiz.q: What was the Prophet ﷺ doing when Umm Hani (RA) came?
o: Performing tawaf
Bathing
Delivering a sermon
Entering the Ka‘bah
quiz.e: Fatimah (RA) had screened him with a cloth (Bukhari 357).

quiz.q: What is the principle behind accepting Umm Hani’s refuge?
o: A special right of members of the Prophet’s household
A general pardon for everyone on the day of victory
A woman’s refuge applies only to close relatives
The Muslims’ covenant is one, even an ordinary person can give it
quiz.e: ‘The covenant of the Muslims is one; even the most ordinary of them can give it’ (Bukhari 3179).

quiz.q: When someone in the family gives someone a promise, what is the lesson of Umm Hani’s incident?
o: My man gave a promise means I myself gave it
The responsibility is only that of the one who gave the promise
A word is invalid without the elders’ permission
A word given by a woman is not binding on men
quiz.e: ‘Whom you have given refuge, we too have given refuge.’

quiz.q: Who came running saying ‘wafa’, not ghadr’?
o: al-Nu‘man ibn Muqarrin (RA)
Ka‘b ibn Malik (RA)
‘Amr ibn ‘Abasah (RA)
Salamah ibn al-Akwa‘ (RA)
quiz.e: Before Mu‘awiyah’s (RA) army (Abu Dawud 2759).

quiz.q: In Anfal 8:58, what does ‘cast the covenant straight back at them’ mean?
o: First announce the cancellation openly
Attack at once at the slightest suspicion
Return the covenant paper to the enemy
Wait until the term ends
quiz.e: Tawdih note 40: a step against the covenant without announcing is a breach of the covenant.

quiz.q: In the incident of Mu‘awiyah’s (RA) army turning back, what was counted as a breach of the covenant?
o: Planning an attack after the term ends
Gathering troops on the border within the term
Sending an envoy to the Romans
Recruiting new soldiers to the army
quiz.e: ‘Neither tighten the knot nor loosen it’; preparation within the term too is forbidden.

quiz.q: What act does ‘war is strategy’ not permit?
o: Confusing the enemy
Hiding one’s real plan from the enemy
Cheating the enemy by breaking a given word
Keeping the real destination secret
quiz.e: Strategy is allowed, but breaking a word given by word is betrayal.

quiz.q: Secretly firming up an arrangement with a new supplier while the contract term remains goes against which lesson?
o: War is strategy
Wafa’, not ghadr
News first, then the foot
Save the arrows

porbos.title: Help from a Non-Muslim • The Rulings That Came at Khaybar • News First, Then the Foot • Ranks, Arrows and Timing • Supplies, Wealth and Tending the Wounded • The Commander-in-Chief • This Chapter in Hanafi Fiqh • Final Word

blocks.1: On the road to Badr, at Harrat al-Wabarah, a man came and joined; he was known for courage and bravery. The Companions were pleased to see him. The man said, I have come to go with you, I will get what is to be got with you. The Prophet {{1}} asked, do you believe in Allah and His Messenger? He said, no. He said,
blocks.3: Then go back; I will not seek the help of a polytheist.{{1}}
blocks.4: On the way he came two more times; both times the same question, the same answer. The third time, arriving at Bayda’, he said, yes, I believe. The Prophet {{1}} said, then come. On the road to Uhud too, a group of Jews, allies of Ibn Ubayy, were turned back with the same words; they did not accept Islam.{{2}}
blocks.5: Yet this same Prophet {{1}} had hired a polytheist of Banu al-Dil to show the way of the hijrah; he had put into his hands his own camel and Abu Bakr’s (RA). That is in dars eleven. And at Hudaybiyah it was Budayl of Khuza‘ah who brought the news of Quraysh, who had not yet become Muslim; Khuza‘ah were the Prophet’s {{2}} trusted well-wishers in Tihamah.{{3}}
blocks.6: Then how do the two statements fit together? The Hanafi jurists, joining the two incidents, have said: help of non-Muslims in fighting will not generally be taken, because the fear of betrayal remains; but if the Muslims are compelled, it may be taken. And in work outside the fighting, such as showing the way, building roads, digging trenches, there is no harm in using the skill of a trustworthy non-Muslim.{{1}}
blocks.7: The Prophet {{1}} turned that man of Badr back three times; in the end he joined the party with faith. The skill of a trustworthy person has value whatever his religion; a polytheist had shown the way of the hijrah. But it is not handing over the reins of one’s own decision to another.
blocks.8: The Rulings That Came at Khaybar
blocks.9: The day of Khaybar. A long siege, a hungry army. People found some donkeys outside the settlement and slaughtered them; meat was boiling in the pots. One came and said, the donkeys are being eaten. The Prophet {{1}} stayed silent. He came again and said it. Again silence. The third time he said, the donkeys are finished! Then the Prophet {{2}} sent a herald. The herald announced,
blocks.11: Allah and His Messenger forbid you the meat of domestic donkeys; for it is impure.{{1}}
blocks.12: At once the pots were overturned; the meat still boiling. A hungry army, the cooking almost done. Yet no one said, let us at least eat today’s. That very day permission for horse meat came; and the prohibition of mut‘ah marriage came.{{1}}
blocks.13: One Sa‘ of Dates for Two Sa‘
blocks.14: After the conquest of Khaybar one man was sent to be in charge there. One day he brought dates of a very fine kind for the Prophet {{1}}. The Prophet {{2}} asked, are all the dates of Khaybar like this? He said, by Allah, no, O Messenger of Allah. We take one sa‘ of these for two sa‘ of mixed dates, two sa‘ for three sa‘. The Prophet {{3}} said,
blocks.16: Do not do this. Sell the mixed dates for dirhams, then with those dirhams buy the fine dates.{{1}}
blocks.17: Taking more or less of the same thing in exchange for the same thing; this is called riba al-fadl, a kind of interest. The prohibition came, and with it the lawful way too. The agreement of half the crop, keeping Khaybar’s land in the Jews’ own hands, and the incident of the poisoned goat will come in dars twenty-one. In the share of spoils too a rule was settled at Khaybar; the mounted fighter received more than the fighter on foot, a separate share for the horse.{{1}}
blocks.18: When a prohibition comes we often say, from next time; this one is already done. The pots of Khaybar were overturned that day while still boiling. And transactions like taking one sa‘ for two sa‘ in the market go on even today; with changed names, changed looks.
blocks.22: Whenever the Messenger of Allah {{1}} intended an expedition, he would conceal the real destination by hinting at another direction.{{2}}
blocks.23: Not a lie; only the real destination was not spoken aloud. The exception was Tabuk. A distant road, fierce heat, a large enemy; so that time everyone was told openly, so that each could prepare. Where secrecy is security, secrecy; where speaking openly is preparation, openly.
blocks.24: And news of the enemy must be known beforehand. At Badr, Busaysah (RA) was sent ahead to look for Abu Sufyan’s caravan. At the Trench Zubayr (RA) went forward again and again to bring news of the enemy; and on that night of cold Hudhayfah (RA) entered the enemy camp. These events have come in earlier dars.{{1}}
blocks.25: The one who was Allah’s Messenger, to whom revelation descended, he too had news brought first, then placed his foot. We decide first, enquire later. A job offer, a talk of marriage, a big purchase; news first, then the foot.
blocks.27: On the day of Badr, the enemy still far. The Prophet {{1}} told the archers,
blocks.29: When they come close to you, then shoot; and save your arrows.{{1}}
blocks.30: Most arrows shot from afar fall on the ground; the quiver empties, the enemy remains unharmed. In one small instruction, the reckoning of supplies and the lesson of patience, together. In the timing of the attack too there was a rule. Nu‘man ibn Muqarrin (RA) said,
blocks.32: I have been present in battle with the Messenger of Allah {{1}}. If he did not fight at the start of the day, he would wait until the winds began to blow and the time of prayer came.{{2}}
blocks.33: The sun declines to the west, the wind blows, the time of prayer comes; and then Allah’s help descends. Three incidents of choosing a place have come in earlier dars. At Badr the camp by the wells, at Uhud fifty archers at the mountain pass, at the Trench the trench. In all three the same thing; if the place is right, half the fight is won in advance.{{1}}
blocks.34: We spend all our strength on the very first blow. The one who is the teacher taught: save your arrows, shoot with timing.
blocks.35: Supplies, Wealth and Tending the Wounded
blocks.36: The Qur’an has given the instruction to prepare like this,
blocks.38: (O Muslims!) Prepare against them whatever strength you can and cavalry stations, by which you will strike fear into the enemy of Allah and your (present) enemy, and others besides them whom you do not know (but) Allah knows them.{{1}}
blocks.39: Strength does not mean only the sword; whatever strength is of use in the age. And the cost of preparation is to be supplied by the whole society. The Prophet {{1}} said,
blocks.41: Whoever equips a fighter in the way of Allah has himself fought; and whoever looks after the family of a fighter in the way of Allah well has fought too.{{1}}
blocks.42: For the one who could not go to the field too, the door is open. Buying one person’s shield; keeping watch over another’s home.
blocks.43: Those Who Drew Water and Bound Wounds
blocks.46: We used to be with the Prophet {{1}}; we would give water to drink, treat the wounded, and bring back the slain to Madinah.{{2}}
blocks.49: I went on seven expeditions with the Messenger of Allah {{1}}. I would stay behind them in the tents, cook food, treat the wounded, tend the sick.{{2}}
blocks.50: At the Trench, for the wounded Sa‘d (RA) a tent was pitched in the mosque itself, so that he could be looked after from close by; that is in dars eighteen.{{1}}
blocks.51: In the work of the religion we know the names of those in the front rows. But the one who drew water, the one who cooked, the one who bound wounds, their words too remain written in the hadith. The work that is not seen is written in the same ledger.
blocks.53: Some people of the Aslam tribe were holding an archery contest. The Prophet {{1}} was passing by them. He said,
blocks.55: O descendants of Isma‘il, shoot; your father too was an archer. Shoot, I am with such-and-such group.{{1}}
blocks.56: The other group stopped their hands. The Prophet {{1}} asked, what happened, why are you not shooting? They said, if you are with their group, how can we shoot! He said, shoot, I am with all of you. In the contest he put his name down with one group; when the other group drew back its hands, he became both groups’. Let training go on, but let no one’s heart be broken. Standing on the minbar he recited that verse of al-Anfal, then said three times,
blocks.58: Know that strength is shooting. Know that strength is shooting. Know that strength is shooting.{{1}}
blocks.59: And he said, whoever learns archery and then gives it up is not of us. The trained horses used to run from al-Hafya’ to Thaniyyat al-Wada‘; the untrained from the Thaniyyah to the mosque of Banu Zurayq.{{1}}
blocks.61: One night a sound of fear rose in Madinah. Anas (RA) told of that night,
blocks.63: The Prophet {{1}} was the most handsome of people, the bravest of people. One night the people of Madinah were frightened and went out toward the sound. On the way the Prophet {{2}} met them; he was already returning with the news, on the bare back of Abu Talhah’s saddleless horse, with a sword hanging from his neck. He was saying, do not be afraid, do not be afraid.{{3}}
blocks.64: While the people were setting out toward the sound, he was already returning with the news. And when the fighting was hardest, al-Bara’ ibn ‘Azib (RA) said,
blocks.66: By Allah, when the fighting grew intense we used to shield ourselves with him. And the brave one among us was the one who could stand beside him.{{1}}
blocks.67: The Companions took shelter behind him; yet he was the Messenger of Allah, whose promise of help had come from the heavens. That promise did not give him leave from preparation. Archery contests, horse races, news of the enemy, the reckoning of saving arrows; he did all of it as a man would.{{1}}
blocks.68: When news of danger comes, it is easy to send others and sit; the one in charge went himself and saw. And tawakkul does not mean giving up preparation; it is trust after preparation.
blocks.70: In brief, the rulings the Hanafi jurists have settled from the incidents of this dars. Fighting those to whom the invitation to Islam has not reached is not permissible before inviting them. Even to those to whom it has reached, inviting first is mustahabb. Jizyah may be taken from the People of the Book, fire-worshippers and non-Arab polytheists; for Arab polytheists, it is either Islam or the sword.
blocks.71: Women, children, decrepit old men, the crippled and the blind may not be killed. But if any of these enters the fighting, takes part by incitement or counsel, or is a leader by whose word people move, even if a woman or child, the ruling is different.
blocks.72: Betrayal, misappropriating spoils and mutilating corpses are haram. If needed, burning the enemy’s fortresses and cutting trees is permissible; when victory is nearly certain it is makruh. Even if there are Muslim prisoners in the enemy fortress, or the enemy makes children a shield, arrows may be shot; but the targets will be only the enemy’s fighters.
blocks.73: The aman given by a free Muslim man or woman to anyone is effective. No attack while a covenant stands; if it is to be broken, it must first be announced openly. One-fifth of the spoils for the set heads, the other four parts for the fighters. In Imam Abu Hanifah’s view the horseman gets two shares, the foot soldier one; in the view of Imam Abu Yusuf and Imam Muhammad the horseman three shares.
blocks.74: The decision on prisoners of war is the ruler’s, looking at the welfare of the Muslims. No one will kill another’s prisoner; taking him to the imam is better. And if bound by any treaty about prisoners, keeping that treaty is necessary.
blocks.75: Help from non-Muslims in fighting should not be taken, but if compelled it may be taken. The meat of the domestic donkey is haram.{{1}}
blocks.77: Some pictures remain from this dars. The two doors kept open before war. A woman killed in the crowd, and one question; this one was not someone to fight! A Caliph walking on foot beside the commander, who did not forget even the beehive.
blocks.78: Before Usamah a question again and again; did you split open his heart? Thumamah released from the mosque pillar, whose hatred became love in three days. A cloak that kept burning as fire. A woman’s refuge, which the Prophet {{1}} accepted as his own refuge. And a horseman’s call; wafa’, not ghadr.
blocks.79: Pots overturned with boiling meat. A commander-in-chief who rode a bare-backed horse and was first to return with news. What a heart that must have been, in whose teaching a Caliph remembered even the enemy’s beehive on a war march! At the very place where there is power yet no accountability, these rules put to the test most of all. So take one deed home from today’s dars.
blocks.81: The Prophet {{1}} bound even the power of the battlefield within limits; no hand on one who is not fighting, no sword if the Kalimah is recited, keeping the word when a word is given. Today I will ask myself a question: in the place where I have power yet no accountability, what kind of person am I really? Today at home, in the shop, or with a subordinate I will stop at such a place, where because of power I could have crossed the limit; I will not give up this stopping from today.

quiz.q: Where did the man who was turned back on the road to Badr first meet them?
o: At Bayda’
At al-Abwa’
At Thaniyyat al-Wada‘ at the edge of Madinah
At Harrat al-Wabarah on the road to Badr
quiz.e: First at Harrat al-Wabarah; the third time at Bayda’ he accepted faith (Muslim 1817).

quiz.q: Turning a polytheist back at Badr, and a polytheist guide on the hijrah; how do the scholars reconcile them?
o: The later event abrogated the earlier
This was a special ruling only for the Prophet ﷺ
Not in war; in peacetime everything is permissible
When compelled in fighting, and there is no harm in other work
quiz.e: al-Kasani: in fighting not generally, but may be taken if compelled; in work outside fighting there is no harm in taking a trustworthy non-Muslim.

quiz.q: In taking on a skilled non-Muslim, what is the dars’s lesson?
o: Never to be taken under any circumstance
If skilled, handing over the whole burden of decisions to him as well
Take him if trustworthy, with the reins of decision in one’s own hand
Taking him only on condition of accepting Islam
quiz.e: A polytheist had shown the way of the hijrah; but authority was the Muslims’.

quiz.q: On hearing the prohibition of donkey meat at Khaybar, what did the Companions do?
o: Overturned the boiling pots
Finished the cooking and ate
Gave the meat away as charity once cooked
Gave it up from the next day
quiz.e: ‘The pots were overturned, the meat still boiling’ (Bukhari 5528).

quiz.q: Against saying ‘this time is done, from next time’ after learning of a prohibition, which picture stands opposite?
o: Thumamah bathing and reciting the Kalimah
Mu‘awiyah’s (RA) army turning back
Stopping the archery contest
Overturning the boiling pots at Khaybar
quiz.e: A hungry army, yet immediate action.

quiz.q: When exchanging an old item at a lower value for a new one, what does the hadith of Khaybar’s dates teach?
o: No more-or-less exchange of the same kind, separate sales
Giving less for a good thing is allowed
If both parties agree, more-or-less exchange of the same kind is allowed
If it is of good quality, taking more is allowed
quiz.e: ‘Sell the mixed dates for dirhams, then buy fine dates with the dirhams.’

quiz.q: In a job offer or a talk of marriage, which lesson of the dars applies?
o: Save the arrows
News first, then the foot
Wafa’, not ghadr
Strength is shooting
quiz.e: Even the one who received revelation had news brought first.

quiz.q: What was the instruction to the archers at Badr?
o: Keep shooting from afar, do not stop
Shoot when they come close, save the arrows
Never give up the mountain pass
Begin shooting only when the wind starts blowing
quiz.e: ‘When they come close, shoot; save your arrows’ (Bukhari 3984).

quiz.q: Against the tendency to spend all one’s strength at the very start of a big task, which instruction stands opposite?
o: No wishing to meet the enemy
War is strategy
Shoot when they come close, save the arrows
Fight steadfastly when you meet the enemy
quiz.e: The instruction at Badr: reckoning of supplies and patience.

quiz.q: On how many expeditions did Umm ‘Atiyyah (RA) go?
o: Three
Five
Seven
Nine
quiz.e: ‘I went on seven expeditions with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ’ (Muslim 1812).

quiz.q: For people who could not go to the field, which door does the dars mention?
o: Only making du‘a from afar
Taking part in the distribution of spoils without going to the field
Sending news of the enemy secretly
Equipping a fighter or looking after his family
quiz.e: ‘He too has fought’ (Bukhari 2843).

quiz.q: When one is given an unseen, behind-the-scenes duty in the religion’s work, what do the incidents of Rubayyi‘ and Umm ‘Atiyyah recall?
o: Unseen work too is written in the same ledger
Front-row work is the real work
Women’s work is limited to inside the home only
The reward for rear work is less
quiz.e: The ones who drew water and bound wounds, their words too are written in the hadith.

quiz.q: On whose horse did the Prophet ﷺ go toward the sound on the night in Madinah?
o: Zubayr’s (RA)
Miqdad ibn al-Aswad’s (RA)
Sa‘d’s (RA)
Abu Talhah’s (RA)
quiz.e: On the bare back of a saddleless horse, a sword at his neck (Bukhari 2908).

quiz.q: As one responsible in an organisation, which model of the Prophet ﷺ can be placed in a crisis?
o: Arranging comfort for everyone first
Going himself to get news of danger
Sending others and waiting himself
Staying silent until news comes
quiz.e: While the people were setting out, he was returning with the news.
